noteBlocks.lede: Several forces pulling one body can always be replaced by a single force that would do exactly the same job. That single force is the resultant, and finding it is the same two-column arithmetic every time: total across, total up.
can: Find the resultant of two or more forces given in i and j form
Resolve forces given at angles and total the two directions
Work out the magnitude and the direction of a resultant

noteBlocks.md: The resultant is the single force with the same effect as the whole set. It has a size and a direction, so an answer is finished only when both are given, or when it is written in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ form. Forces pulling different ways never simply add up: their directions decide the total.

noteBlocks.stem: Two forces of 11 N and 6 N act at a point. How big can their resultant be?

steps.decision: Pulling together, the whole of each counts: the largest the resultant can be.
Pulling against each other, the smaller cancels part of the larger: the smallest it can be.
Any other direction gives a size between those two.

noteBlocks.prompt: Forces of 35 N and 12 N act at a point in different directions. Which could be the size of their resultant?
noteBlocks.explain: In different directions the resultant lies between the difference, $35 - 12 = 23$ N, and the sum, $47$ N, as steps 1 and 2 of See it showed; 47 N needs both to point the same way, so 37 N is the only one possible.

twin.prompt: Forces of 20 N and 9 N act at a point in different directions. Which could be the size of their resultant?
twin.explain: Between the difference, 11 N, and the sum, 29 N; the sum itself needs both to point the same way.

optionNotes.why: 29 N is their sum, which needs both forces to point the same way; in different directions the resultant is less.
That is more than their sum, 29 N, and no pair of 20 N and 9 N can make more than that.
47 N is their sum, which needs both forces to point the same way; in different directions part of each works against the other.
That is more than their sum, 47 N, and no pair of 35 N and 12 N can make more than that.

noteBlocks.text: In i and j: total each column

noteBlocks.md: When the forces are given in components the work is arithmetic: total the $\mathbf{i}$ parts, total the $\mathbf{j}$ parts, and keep the two columns apart. Watch the negatives: adding $-5$ takes five away, and subtracting a force instead of adding it is a slip the reports have seen here.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the resultant of $(5\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-8\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ N and $(6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N.

steps.decision: Total the i column on its own, each number with its sign.
Then the j column, separately: nothing crosses between them.
The two totals side by side are the resultant in i and j form.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two forces are $(10\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-7\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N. What is their resultant?
noteBlocks.explain: Column by column, as See it did: $10 - 7 = 3$ across and $-2 + 6 = 4$ up, so the resultant is $3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$ N. Subtracting the second force instead of adding it is the slip to avoid.

twin.prompt: Two forces are $(9\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-5\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})$ N. What is their resultant?
twin.answer: 4i - 2j | 4i-2j | 4i − 2j | 4i - 2j N | 4i-2j N | -2j + 4i | R = 4i - 2j | (4i - 2j) N | (4i - 2j) | 4i - 2j newtons | 4 i - 2 j

noteBlocks.md: Forces given at angles are resolved before they are combined. Take to the right and upwards as positive, resolve every force into those two directions, then total each direction. A force pointing left or down counts negative in its total.

noteBlocks.stem: Three forces pull a point: 26 N to the right, 15 N at 40° above the horizontal to the right, and 8 N to the left. Total each direction.

steps.decision: Right positive: the 8 N force points left, so it is subtracted.
The two horizontal forces have no upward part.

noteBlocks.prompt: A force of 20 N acts horizontally to the right and a force of 6 N acts horizontally to the left. What is the total component to the right, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: The second force points the other way, so it is subtracted, as the 8 N force was in step 1 of See it: $20 - 6 = 14$ N.

twin.prompt: A force of 17 N acts horizontally to the right and a force of 23 N acts horizontally to the left. What is the total component to the right, in newtons?
twin.explain: $17 - 23 = -6$ N: the total is negative because the larger force points left.

noteBlocks.caption: The two totals are the legs; the resultant is the longest side.

noteBlocks.md: The across total and the up total are at right angles, so they are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle and the resultant is its longest side. That makes the magnitude $\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, on the Unit 2 formula sheet as the magnitude of $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$.
Keep the totals unrounded in the calculator until the last line. Rounding a total before squaring it can move the second decimal place of the magnitude, and the mark for the value goes with it.

noteBlocks.stem: The forces on a body total 16 N across and 12 N up. Find the magnitude of the resultant.

steps.decision: The two totals are the shorter sides; the resultant is the longest.
Square, add, then take the square root: the root is the step most often left off.

noteBlocks.prompt: The forces on a body have a total component of 8 N to the right and 6 N upwards. What is the magnitude of the resultant, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: The two totals are perpendicular, so Pythagoras applies, as in See it: $\sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ N. Adding them, 14 N, treats them as pulling the same way.

noteBlocks.md: In the same triangle the up total is opposite the angle with the horizontal and the across total is beside it, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{Y}{X}$: the angle with the horizontal, the line these questions almost always name.
Name the line in the answer, as in '28.07° above the horizontal'. A resultant pointing down or to the left still takes the inverse tangent of the two sizes; the sketch says which way it points.

noteBlocks.title: Why the fraction goes that way up
noteBlocks.md: Tangent is opposite over adjacent. Measuring from the horizontal makes the up total the opposite side and the across total the adjacent one, so the up total goes on top.

noteBlocks.stem: A resultant has totals of 15 N across and 8 N up. Find the angle it makes with the horizontal.

steps.decision: The up total is opposite the angle, so it goes on top.
Name the line it is measured from.
The fraction turned over gives the angle with the vertical, a different answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: A resultant has a total component of $X$ to the right and $Y$ upwards. Which expression gives the angle it makes with the horizontal?
noteBlocks.explain: The up total is opposite the angle with the horizontal and the across total beside it, as in step 1 of See it, so the up total goes on top. Turning the fraction over gives the angle with the vertical.

twin.prompt: A resultant has a total component of $X$ to the right and $Y$ upwards. Which expression gives the angle it makes with the vertical?
twin.explain: Measured from the vertical, the across total is opposite the angle, so it goes on top.

optionNotes.why: That is the angle with the horizontal; measured from the vertical, the across total is opposite the angle and goes on top.
Cosine compares a side with the longest side, the resultant; the two totals compared with each other give a tangent.
That is the fraction turned over, which gives the angle with the vertical rather than the horizontal.
Sine compares a side with the longest side, the resultant; the two totals compared with each other give a tangent.

noteBlocks.md: **The missing force** (2023). The resultant is given and one force is not: take the forces you know away from the resultant, column by column. **Both parts at once** (every year): a part may ask for the resultant in $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ and then its magnitude and direction, each using the one before.
**An angle turned into i and j**: a force given by its size and angle is written in components first, then added in columns.

noteBlocks.stem: $(6\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})$ N is the resultant of $(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{c}$. Find $\mathbf{c}$.

steps.decision: The three forces add to R, so c is what is left once a and b are taken away.
Column by column, each sign reversed as it is taken away.
Check: a + b + c gives R back.

noteBlocks.prompt: The resultant of $(3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ N and a third force $\mathbf{c}$ is $(5\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})$ N. What is $\mathbf{c}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Take the known forces from the resultant, as in See it: across $5 - 3 + 1 = 3$, up $1 - 2 - 4 = -5$, so $\mathbf{c} = 3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}$ N. Adding them all would give the resultant of four forces.

twin.prompt: The resultant of $(3\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$ N, $(2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})$ N and a third force $\mathbf{c}$ is $(9\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N. What is $\mathbf{c}$?
twin.answer: 4i + 4j | 4i+4j | 4j + 4i | 4i + 4j N | 4i+4j N | c = 4i + 4j | (4i + 4j) N | (4i + 4j) | 4i + 4j newtons | 4 i + 4 j

noteBlocks.text: An unknown part from the magnitude

noteBlocks.md: **A magnitude given** (2021). The size is given and one part is unknown: square both parts, add, and set the total equal to the size squared. The equation gives two roots; the question's picture or wording says which sign to keep.

noteBlocks.stem: A resultant force $(x\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ N has a magnitude of 10 N. Find $x$.

steps.decision: The magnitude squared is the sum of the two parts squared.
Take the known part's square away.
Both roots fit the size; keep the one the question asks for.

workedExamples.stem:
Throughout, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular unit vectors, with $\mathbf{i}$ along the positive x-axis.

Three forces act on a body: $(9\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ N, $(-5\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N and $(8\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N.

(i) Find the resultant of the three forces.
(ii) Calculate its magnitude.
(iii) Calculate the angle it makes with the positive x-axis. Round to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: Total one column at a time. Adding $-5$ takes five away, which is where the sign slips happen.

steps.working: So the resultant is $12\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}$ N, since the $\mathbf{j}$ parts give $-4 + 7 + 2 = 5$.
steps.decision: Nothing crosses between the columns, so the second total is worked out on its own and then written beside the first.

options: Because across and up are independent directions
Because the two columns must be added together at the end
Because the resultant is always a single number
whyMenu.explain: A step to the right never moves you up, so the two totals stay apart. The single number comes later, as the magnitude.

steps.decision: The two totals are perpendicular, so the magnitude is the longest side of their right-angled triangle.

steps.working: Measured from the positive x-axis, the angle $= \tan^{-1}\dfrac{5}{12} = 22.62°$.
steps.decision: The up total is opposite the angle, so it goes on top. Measuring from the x-axis is what the question asked for.

twin.stem:
A body has a total component of $24$ N to the right and $7$ N upwards. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant.

Answer ________ N

items.stem: From an earlier topic: work out $-4 + 7 + 2$.

options.feedback: Adding 7 to $-4$ gives 3, and 2 more gives 5.
That treats the $-4$ as $+4$.
That subtracts both of the other numbers.
That leaves the 2 out.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a right-angled triangle has shorter sides of $8$ and $6$. How long is the longest side?

options.feedback: That adds the two sides, which would only be right if they pointed the same way.
That is the sum of the squares, before the square root.
That doubles each side instead of squaring it: $2 \times 8 + 2 \times 6 = 28$.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: in a right-angled triangle the side opposite an angle is $5$ and the side beside it is $12$. Which expression gives the angle?

options.feedback: Tangent is opposite over adjacent, so the 5 goes on top.
That is the other angle in the same triangle.
Sine needs the longest side underneath, not the adjacent one.
That would take the tangent of a number rather than finding the angle.

items.stem: Two forces of $11$ N and $4$ N act at a point. Which of these could NOT be the size of their resultant?

options.feedback: The largest a resultant can be is $11 + 4 = 15$ N, when both point the same way. 16 N is impossible.
15 N is possible: it is the resultant when both forces point the same way.
10 N is possible: at some angle between them the resultant takes any size from 7 N to 15 N.
7 N is possible: it is the resultant when the forces point opposite ways, $11 - 4$.

items.stem: What is the resultant of $(7\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-4\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ N?

options.feedback: $7 - 4 = 3$ across and $-3 + 8 = 5$ up.
That subtracts the second force instead of adding it.
The $-3$ has lost its sign: adding 8 to $-3$ gives 5, not 11.
The $-4$ has lost its sign: adding it takes four away.

items.stem: One force has a component of $18$ N to the right and another has a component of $25$ N to the left. What is the total component to the right?
items.skill: Totalling components that face each other

options.feedback: $18 - 25 = -7$ N, so the total of 7 N actually points to the left.
Adding treats the second component as helping the first.
The size is right but the sign is not: taking right as positive, the total is negative.
Components are added and subtracted, never multiplied.

items.stem: The forces on a body total $24$ N to the right and $10$ N upwards. What is the magnitude of the resultant?

options.feedback: That adds the two totals. They act at right angles, so the resultant is shorter than their sum.
That is the sum of the squares. The square root is the last step.
That is the larger total on its own, with the other one left out.

items.stem: The forces on a body total $24$ N to the right and $10$ N upwards. Which expression gives the angle the resultant makes with the horizontal?

options.feedback: The up total is opposite the angle and the across total beside it, so the up total goes on top.
That is the angle with the vertical. The reports name this reciprocal as the commonest error in the direction part.
Sine needs the resultant, 26 N, underneath.
Cosine also needs the resultant underneath, and it would give the angle from the other side.

findTheMistake.stem: Rhys is finding the resultant of the forces $(6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $(-5\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ N. His working:
studentWorking: the resultant is the sum of the forces
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 subtracts the second force's $\mathbf{j}$ part where line 1 says the forces are added. The $\mathbf{i}$ line is right: $-5$ is already negative, so adding it takes five away. The $\mathbf{j}$ line should add 9 to $-2$ and give 7.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the resultant as the sum and keeping the two columns apart is the method, and it earns the method mark (M). One operation applies to the whole vector: if the i line adds, the j line adds too. Writing the two forces one above the other before you start makes a stray sign hard to miss.

findTheMistake.stem: Seán wants the angle the resultant $(8\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N makes with the horizontal. His working:
studentWorking: the angle comes from an inverse tangent
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 has the fraction upside down. Measured from the horizontal, the up total, 5, is opposite the angle and goes on top; 57.99° is the angle with the vertical.
findTheMistake.feedback: Choosing the inverse tangent is the method, and it earns the method mark (M). Sketch the triangle and mark the angle: the side opposite it goes on top.

prompts.prompt: What is the resultant of a set of forces?
prompts.answer: The single force that would have exactly the same effect on the body as the whole set.

prompts.prompt: Forces are given at angles. What is the first step?
prompts.answer: Resolve every force into two perpendicular directions, usually the horizontal and the vertical.

prompts.prompt: Totals X across and Y up: what is the resultant's magnitude?
prompts.answer: The square root of X squared plus Y squared, which is on the Unit 2 formula sheet.

prompts.prompt: Why can 30 N, 24 N and 10 N not give 64 N unless parallel?
prompts.answer: Because forces only add to their total when they point the same way; otherwise part of each works against the others.

prompts.prompt: What is the commonest slip when finding a resultant's direction?
